claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy undergoes a crossover from dislocation-slip-dominated plasticity at higher temperatures and lower strain rates to twin-mediated plasticity at lower temperatures and higher strain rates.
Twin-mediated plasticity enhances both strength and ductility through increased work hardening from twin boundaries.
The solid-solutionized Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy has a homogenized, single-phase FCC microstructure.
The Co-free alloy has a grain size comparable to that of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is an FCC alloy.
Reducing temperature lowers the stacking-fault energy of Co-free FeNiCrMn and promotes deformation-twin nucleation and growth.
Increasing strain rate lowers the effective stacking-fault energy or otherwise promotes deformation-twin nucleation and growth in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
As temperature decreases, partial-dislocation activity and stacking-fault stability increase the prevalence of deformation twins.
As strain rate increases, partial-dislocation activity and stacking-fault stability increase the prevalence of deformation twins.
Twin boundaries act as planar barriers to dislocation motion in the Co-free alloy.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate deformation will produce a substantial increase in twin-boundary density and work hardening relative to higher-temperature or lower-rate deformation.
The low-temperature, high-strain-rate condition will yield higher strength and ductility than the predominantly slip-based baseline.
At moderate or high temperatures and lower strain rates, Co-free FeNiCrMn exhibits dislocation-only plasticity with reduced strain hardening.
Below approximately −50 °C, thermally sensitive stacking-fault energy may limit twinning and diminish its work-hardening contribution.
Above approximately 500–600 °C, diffusion or other rate-limiting mechanisms may suppress the contribution of twinning.
The slip-to-twinning transition threshold can vary with subtle composition or microstructural changes.

A controlled temperature-and-strain-rate comparison using stress–strain data, twin-sensitive diffraction, and post-test microscopy can test whether increased twinning coincides with increased work hardening.

contradictions.description: The central prediction says decreasing temperature promotes twinning, including tests down to −100 °C, whereas the boundary says temperatures below approximately −50 °C may limit twinning. No intervening optimum or non-monotonic temperature dependence is specified to reconcile these statements.
